title: Quiz: Binary Logic & Numbers - Advanced
prompt: Test your advanced understanding of bitfield extractions, two's complement anomalies, and shift mechanics.

questions.question: Why is the Arithmetic Shift Right (ASR) instruction required when dividing a negative signed integer by a power of two?
options: Because LSR will trigger an arithmetic exception on negative numbers.
Because ASR duplicates the sign bit during the shift (sign extension), whereas LSR shifts a 0 into the leftmost bit, destroying the negative sign.
Because ASR automatically rounds up the lost remainder.
Because ASR uses the 64-bit X registers while LSR only uses W registers.
questions.explanation: ASR preserves the sign by duplicating the sign bit when shifting. If you use LSR on a negative number, a 0 is inserted at the left, destroying the sign and corrupting the value.
questions.hint: Think about what happens to the left-most bit (the sign bit) when you shift bits to the right.

questions.question: The standard `mov Xd, Xm` instruction is actually an alias for which logical operation?
options: orr Xd, xzr, Xm
and Xd, xzr, Xm
eor Xd, xzr, Xm
add Xd, xzr, Xm
questions.explanation: mov Xd, Xm is an alias for orr Xd, xzr, Xm (Inclusive OR with the Zero Register).
questions.hint: Moving a value unchanged is the equivalent of combining it with zero using an Inclusive OR.

questions.question: What is the primary difference between the `bfi` (Bitfield Insert) and `ubfiz` (Unsigned Bitfield Insert in Zero) instructions?
options: bfi clears the source register, while ubfiz does not.
bfi replaces only the target bitfield and leaves other bits in Wd unchanged, whereas ubfiz zeroes out the entire Wd register first.
ubfiz sign-extends the bits on the left, while bfi does not.
bfi can only operate on 64-bit registers.
questions.explanation: ubfiz is similar to bfi, except that the destination register (Wd) is zeroed first, rather than leaving the non-targeted bits unchanged.
questions.hint: The 'z' in the instruction name stands for 'Zero'.

questions.question: What does the instruction `bfxil Wd, Wn, #lsb, #width` do to the un-targeted bits in the destination register `Wd`?
options: It zero-extends them.
It sign-extends them.
It leaves all other bits in Wd unchanged.
It flips them using a NOT operation.
questions.explanation: In Bitfield Extract and Insert Low (bfxil), bits 0 to (width - 1) in Wd are replaced by the source bitfield, and all other bits in Wd are unchanged.
questions.hint: This instruction 'inserts' into the low bits without destroying the rest of the existing data in the destination.

questions.question: When converting a negative number to its positive counterpart in two's complement, what happens if you apply the negation steps (one's complement + 1) to -5 (1011 in 4-bit)?
options: It generates an overflow error.
It results in 0101, which is exactly +5.
It results in 0100, which requires a separate sign bit change.
The operation fails because negation only works from positive to negative.
questions.explanation: The negation process (one's complement + 1) works identically in both directions. The one's complement of 1011 (-5) is 0100. Adding 1 results in 0101 (+5).
questions.hint: The algorithm is symmetrical regardless of which direction you are converting.
